newsitem.title: USA: World Bank advising dozen countries on corruption.
newsitem.headline: World Bank advising dozen countries on corruption.

text.p: The World Bank is working with a dozen countries in Latin America, Africa and Asia to develop anticorruption programs, World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday.

Citing studies conducted by Harvard University, Wolfensohn said at a news conference that corruption has become the biggest single issue on the minds of voters and the greatest inhibiting factor for investments in developing nations.
Wolfensohn said the World Bank was encouraging member countries to sign on to a pledge against bribery to cover projects financed with bank resources.

"But the major impact will only come when the governments stand up and say it. The governments have to say it, not only by setting up some committee but at the very highest level. If it is not cured at the top corruption doesn't cease," he said.
Wolfensohn mentioned Ukraine President Leonid Kuchma as an example of a head of state who had spoken out and taken public action against corruption.

The Australian-born banker caused a stir last year when he lashed out against corruption in industrialized and developing countries, comparing it to a cancer and vowing to pull out of any project tainted by wrongdoing.

Since then, Wolfensohn said, the issue has become a principal topic of political debate in countries all around the world, and governments are already feeling pressure from their own people to address the problem.

"People don't like being poor, but they're prepared to put up with it if there's a future and if there's not inequity," he said . But if they see a lot of people creaming money off the top, that gets them mad. And that's been shown in country after country".
The World Bank can help governments address one source of corruption by advising them on deregulation, since state controls often create chances for venality, he said.
It has also held training workshops on anti-corruption strategies for legislators, civil servants and journalists in regional meetings in Africa, Asia, Central America and the Middle East.
However, Wolfensohn stressed that the decision to combat corruption must come from the governments, since the bank has no power or mandate to police them.
